name: Jamal Quinn

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, Jamal, and thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I drive the shearer on a longwall at an underground coal mine. A longwall is a coal face about three hundred metres long, with a row of hydraulic roof supports holding the roof up, and the shearer is the cutting machine that runs up and down the face taking a slice of coal each pass. I'm the crew lead on my shift, so I look after eight men and two women at the face. We go down at six, do our checks, and then it's cutting, watching the roof, watching the gas, and keeping the conveyor moving. I like the teamwork; a good longwall crew moves like one body. What wears me out is the heat and the noise, and getting home too tired to talk to Grace.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Has the longwall changed in your time?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Massively. The roof supports move forward on their own now, and the shearer can do automatic passes with us watching from further back. Half my job is watching a screen on the face and stepping in when the machine gets it wrong. The machine does the easy passes now, and I do the hard ones, which is fine until the machine learns the hard ones too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, the world's still got sense in it. At church I'd say hard work still counts for something. I don't post much online, maybe the odd thing on the church page.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it means our longwall keeps going on the same path it was on: more automation bit by bit, but a crew still needed. I'd get to sixty-five, God willing. That's all I've asked for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep doing my job and keep mentoring the apprentices. I'd try to put some money by, maybe start fixing lawnmowers in the garage on weekends again for a bit extra. Nothing dramatic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Grateful, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why is there so little saved, as a crew lead?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The company's been struggling, so our pay's been frozen three years while everything costs more. And our daughter came home with her two boys after her divorce last year. We've got six at the dinner table on a pay that hasn't moved since 2023, and I wouldn't trade a single chair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you use AI tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now and then. My grandson showed me how to ask it to tidy up the church newsletter, and it did a decent job. I wouldn't trust it with anything that matters, but for commas it's fine.

S0.say: The world's still got sense in it, and hard work still counts for something. He'd say it at church and maybe on the church page online.
S0.think: Our longwall keeps automating bit by bit, but a crew is still needed. I'd get to sixty-five, God willing, which is all I've asked for.
S0.do: Keeps working and mentoring apprentices, and tries to save by fixing lawnmowers in the garage on weekends. Makes no dramatic changes.
S0.quote: We've got six at the dinner table on a pay that hasn't moved since 2023, and I wouldn't trade a single chair.
S0.fieldNote: Jamal is a crew lead and church man who already works alongside a semi-automated longwall. His thin savings come from a three-year pay freeze and taking in his daughter and grandsons, which he would not change. He uses AI lightly and only for small things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say change is part of life and we have to meet it. The companies need to compete, and if they don't automate, a mine somewhere else will and we'll close anyway. What they owe us is proper apprenticeships for the new skills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think the longwall would be run from the surface for most shifts, with a small crew going down for maintenance. I might be one of the ones kept, because I know the face. But my crew of ten would become a crew of three.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Once the first lot of surface operators had shown it works, I'd take the training. I'd start the lawnmower repairs properly, with a sign out front. And I'd talk to the apprentices about which skills will last, like electrical and hydraulics.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy. I believe it can work out, but I don't like thinking about who'd be left.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a crew of ten becomes three. How would you choose, if they asked you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd pray about it first, honestly. Then I'd look at who has kids at home and who has another trade to fall back on. I've led men into a face with the roof talking, and nothing frightens me like being asked to pick who goes home for good.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you think the government should step in to protect jobs?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not to stop the machines, no. That just props up something that can't last. But they could help pay for apprenticeships so people can earn while they learn, that's money well spent.

S1.say: Change is part of life: companies must compete or a mine elsewhere will automate and we'll close anyway. What they owe workers is proper apprenticeships for the new skills.
S1.think: The longwall would mostly be run from the surface, with a small crew going down for maintenance. I might be kept, but my crew of ten would become three.
S1.do: Takes the surface operator training once the first group has shown it works. Starts lawnmower repairs properly with a sign out front and advises apprentices on lasting skills like electrical and hydraulics.
S1.feel: A bit uneasy, believing it can work out but not liking to think who would be left.
S1.quote: I've led men into a face with the roof talking, and nothing frightens me like being asked to pick who goes home for good.
S1.fieldNote: Jamal accepts automation on free-market grounds but wants government money for apprenticeships. His real dread is being asked to choose which crew members go. He'd move once others prove the system, in keeping with his steady approach.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say families and churches will have to carry each other, because no government can move fast enough for this. I'd say it from the pulpit if they let me. And I'd say the companies should keep faith with the men who built them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Just between us, it scares me. Two years and I'm sixty, with six at the table and a mortgage. If even the surface jobs are gone, my training is worth nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get the lawnmower and small engine repairs going full time on weekends, and ask my son-in-law, who's out of work, to help. We'd cut everything back, the cable, the car, the holiday. I'd ask the church to set up a fund for mining families, and I'd put my name on the roster to help run it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. The kind of worry that wakes you at three in the morning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does two years take away that five or ten wouldn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Time to train. With five or ten I'd get my surface ticket and ride it out. With two years, there's no ticket to get. The surface goes the same day as the face.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the lawnmower business really carry a family of six?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, not alone. But it would keep food on the table with Grace's daycare. And it would keep me useful, which matters to a man. I'd rather fix a mower for twenty than sit and wait for a cheque.

S2.say: Families and churches will have to carry each other, because no government can move fast enough for this. Companies should keep faith with the men who built them.
S2.think: Two years and I'm sixty with six at the table and a mortgage. If even the surface jobs go, my training is worth nothing.
S2.do: Turns the lawnmower and small engine repairs into a full weekend business with his son-in-law. Cuts cable, a car and the holiday, and helps the church set up and run a fund for mining families.
S2.feel: Alarmed, the kind of worry that wakes him at three in the morning.
S2.quote: With two years, there's no ticket to get. The surface goes the same day as the face.
S2.fieldNote: The two-year picture removes the surface training route that steadied Jamal. He turns to self-reliance through his repair business and to church support rather than government. Staying useful matters to him as much as the money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a fair warning, so let's not waste it. I'd tell my crew to get a second trade going and the company to pay for the apprenticeships. That's the sensible road.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years and I'm sixty-three. I think I could get the surface ticket, work there a few years, and leave close to sixty-five. The lawnmower business would cover the gap if there is one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one, I'd do the surface operator course as soon as the first group's settled in. I'd build the repair business slowly, a few jobs a week, so it's running by the time I need it. Any extra would go on the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I'd feel like I'm steering.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd wait for the first group even with five years. Isn't that time lost?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe six months, but I've seen too many new systems fail at first. I'd rather be second and right than first and wrong. Grace calls me the slowest early adopter in town.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the apprentices you mentor?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them to learn the hydraulics and the electrics, because somebody has to fix the robots. I'd tell them the robots will need nurses, and nurses with grease on their hands get paid.

S3.say: Five years is a fair warning, so let's not waste it. He'd tell his crew to get a second trade going and the company to pay for apprenticeships.
S3.think: Five years puts me at sixty-three, so I could get the surface ticket and leave near sixty-five. The lawnmower business would cover any gap.
S3.do: Does the surface operator course once the first group has settled, building the repair business slowly in the meantime. Puts any extra money on the mortgage.
S3.quote: I'd tell them the robots will need nurses, and nurses with grease on their hands get paid.
S3.fieldNote: With five years Jamal sees a workable path through surface operations and his repair business. He still prefers to go second rather than first, and laughs at himself about it. His advice to apprentices centres on fixing the machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a blessing, if people use it. Train the young, keep the old ones on until they're done, and let the market sort out the rest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years and I'm sixty-eight, so I'm out. My grandsons will be teenagers then, and that's who I'd worry about. For me, it's the gentle one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep working, keep mentoring, retire at sixty-five. Build up the repair business so it's something I can do in retirement. Maybe teach my grandsons to fix engines on Saturdays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, for the boys, not for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want your grandsons to know?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That hands and character still matter. I'd teach those boys to strip a carburettor so they know a machine isn't magic, it's just parts somebody put together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would ten years change how you lead your crew?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk more openly with them about what's coming. I'd encourage the young ones to take every course on offer. And I'd make sure nobody felt they were going to be dropped without warning.

S4.say: Ten years is a blessing, if people use it: train the young, keep the old ones on until they're done, and let the market sort out the rest.
S4.think: By 2036 I'm sixty-eight and out, so for me it's the gentle one. My grandsons will be teenagers, and they're who I'd worry about.
S4.do: Keeps working and mentoring, and plans to retire at sixty-five. Builds the repair business as a retirement activity and teaches his grandsons engine repair on Saturdays.
S4.feel: Uneasy for his grandsons, not for himself.
S4.quote: I'd teach those boys to strip a carburettor so they know a machine isn't magic, it's just parts somebody put together.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade Jamal feels personally safe and focuses on his grandsons and crew. He would lead more openly about what's coming. The carburettor line shows how he connects practical skill with character.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Six at the table, a mortgage, and no time to get the surface ticket. What would help is the company keeping older workers on until their pension and paying for apprenticeships so younger people can earn while they learn. Not handouts, real work.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the crew. Underground, the crew is family. I'd want any change to keep people together as long as possible, not scatter them one at a time.

headlineQuote: The machine does the easy passes now, and I do the hard ones, which is fine until the machine learns the hard ones too.
portrait: Jamal Quinn is a 58-year-old longwall shearer driver and crew lead at an underground coal mine, already working beside machines that make automatic passes. A three-year pay freeze and taking in his daughter and two grandsons have left him with almost nothing saved. He is a traditional church man who accepts automation on free-market grounds but wants apprenticeships, and he waits for others to prove new systems before moving. Slower scenarios leave him uneasy or anxious with a plan built on surface training and a small engine repair business, while two years alarms him because the surface jobs would vanish too.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because with six at the table and a mortgage there would be no time to get the surface operator ticket.
whatWouldHelp: The company keeping older workers on until their pensions and paying for apprenticeships so younger people can earn while they learn.
